text.p: German sportswear maker adidas AG said on Wednesday it was confident of beating its 1996 record results this year and expressed interest in reviewing share buyback plans and raising its future dividend payouts.

Adidas Chief Executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus, announcing he also wanted to stay on at the helm of the company through the turn of the century, said the group would meet the expectations of investors with its 1997 results.

"All in all, we are confident that our business prospects for the full year are very favourable for ensuring further steady growth in sales and profitability, and thus living up to the expectations of our investors and the financial community," he told the group's annual general meeting in Nuremberg.

Louis-Dreyfus said the order backlog at the end of March was indicative of the group's strength, having risen 36 percent in the first quarter compared with the 1996 quarter. Surging apparel sales, followed by footwear, were behind the growth.
Adidas, famous for its three-stripe logo, reported a 43 percent rise in first quarter net sales to 1.7 billion marks ($998.4 million), while pre-tax profit rose 42 percent to 243 million marks.
Net sales for 1996 rose 35 percent to 4.7 billion marks, while pre-tax profit rose 50 percent to 444 million marks.

The positive outlook for 1997 underpinned adidas shares in bourse trade. They reached a new record high at 191.50 marks before slipping along with the rest of the German share market to end the session down 30 pfennigs at 189.20 marks.
Louis-Dreyfus said adidas was interested in share buyback proposals once they become applicable under German law.
"We consider share buybacks as an interesting concept to provide shareholders with cash and at the same time potentially increase the value of the adidas share," Louis-Dreyfus said.
"We believe that our industry offers ample growth opportunities which can provide shareholders with attractive value enhancement for their funds invested."

He also defended adidas' dividend payout policy despite criticism from some German shareholder groups, saying it was in line with the policy outlined by adidas when it was floated in November 1995 and also with dividends of major competitors.
Adidas had proposed a 1996 net dividend of 1.10 marks per share, which was a payout ratio of 16 percent of net income.
But Louis-Dreyfus hinted at the prospects for higher dividend payouts in the coming years.

"As the financial leverage in our balance sheet continues to decline, we will certainly look into the possibility to increase dividend payments, and analyse in detail other options available, to redeem shareholders and adjust our capital structure."

Louis-Dreyfus, who has engineered the turnaround of adidas after leading the group of investors which bought the troubled group in the mid-1990s, also said he would like to remain on the management board through the turn of the century.
"I would like to be on the management board in 2000 if the shareholders don't sack me," he said at the meeting.

Louis-Dreyfus had said at recent news conferences that he would step down and join the supervisory board after the 1998 World Cup. He did not specifically explain at the meeting on Wednesday why he wanted to stay on the management board. ($ = 1.702 German Marks)
